slides.title: Title Slide: Introduction to Tokens and Tokenization
slides.narration: Welcome to this Spoken Tutorial on Introduction to **Tokens** and **Tokenization**.

slides.title: Learning Objectives
slides.narration:
In this tutorial, you will learn to explain what **tokens** are.
Understand how **tokenization** works.
And identify why **tokens** are crucial for **LLM** performance, cost, and efficiency.

slides.title: System Requirements
slides.narration:
Here I am using a browser on a computer or mobile.
We will also use an online **tokenizer** tool.

slides.title: Pre-requisite Slide
slides.narration:
To follow this tutorial, you must be connected to the internet.
You should also be familiar with **Generative AI** and **Prompting**.

slides.title: What are Tokens?
content: LLMs don't read words like humans.
slides.narration:
**LLMs** don't read words like humans do.
They process text in small chunks called **tokens**.
Think of **tokens** as the fundamental building blocks of language for an **AI**.
It's like breaking down a long sentence into individual LEGO blocks.
Let's see this with an example using an online **tokenizer** tool.
Open your browser and search for an online **tokenizer**.
Many free tools are available.
Type the word "The" into the **tokenizer**.
Notice it often appears as one **token**.
Now type "Tokenization".
Observe how it might be split into multiple **tokens**, like "Token", "iz", and "ation".
This shows how an **LLM** breaks down text into pieces it can understand.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration of LEGO blocks forming a sentence, then a screenshot of an online tokenizer showing "The" as one token and "Tokenization" as multiple tokens.

slides.title: How Tokenization Works
content: Splits raw text into sub-word pieces.
slides.narration:
The **tokenizer** acts like a special dictionary for the **LLM**.
It knows how to split raw text into these sub-word **tokens**.
It's like a chef chopping vegetables into specific sizes for a recipe.
Let's continue with our **tokenizer** tool.
Type "Hello, how are you today?"
See how the **tokenizer** splits words, punctuation, and spaces into separate **tokens**.
For example, "Hello", ",", " ", "how", " ", "are", " ", "you", " ", "today", "?".
This process, called **tokenization**, is how an **LLM** prepares text for understanding.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration of a dictionary or a chef chopping vegetables, then a screenshot of an online tokenizer showing "Hello, how are you today?" split into multiple tokens.

slides.title: Why Tokens Matter: Context Windows
content: Measured in fixed number of tokens.
slides.narration:
Now, why should you care about **tokens**?
First, consider the **LLM's** **context window**.
Think of the **context window** as an **LLM's** short-term memory.
It's like a small whiteboard where the **LLM** can only see a limited number of words at once.
This memory is measured in a fixed number of **tokens**, for example, 8,192 **tokens**.
Go back to your **tokenizer** tool.
Paste a long paragraph, perhaps from a news article.
Observe the **token** count displayed by the tool.
If your text exceeds the **LLM's** **context window** limit, it simply gets cut off.
This means the **LLM** cannot "remember" or process everything you give it beyond that **token** limit.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration of a whiteboard with limited space, then a screenshot of an online tokenizer showing a long paragraph and its token count.

slides.title: Why Tokens Matter: Cost
content: Efficient RAG systems use fewer tokens.
slides.narration:
Second, **tokens** directly impact the cost of using **LLMs**.
**API** providers charge you per **token** processed.
It's like a taxi meter that charges you for every mile you travel.
More miles, more cost.
Let's use our **tokenizer** again.
Type a short sentence, then a very long paragraph.
Notice the difference in **token** count.
A system like **RAG**, or **Retrieval Augmented Generation**, aims to be more efficient.
It can reduce the number of **tokens** sent to the **LLM**.
Fewer **tokens** mean significantly cheaper operations, especially at scale.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration of a taxi meter, then a screenshot of an online tokenizer showing token counts for a short sentence versus a long paragraph.

slides.title: Why Tokens Matter: Chunking
slides.narration:
Finally, **tokens** are vital for **chunking** your documents.
When preparing large documents for an **LLM**, we often break them into smaller pieces called **chunks**.
Think of **chunking** a book into individual chapters or sections.
Each **chunk** needs to fit within the **LLM's** **context window**.
Imagine you have a large **PDF** document.
Before sending it to an **LLM**, you would split it into smaller **chunks**.
Each of these **chunks** must be measured in **tokens**.
This ensures that the **LLM** can process each part without exceeding its memory limit.
Understanding **tokens** helps you manage and optimize your data effectively.
slides.image_prompt: Illustration of a book being divided into chapters, then a visual representation of a document being chunked into token-measured segments.

slides.title: Summary
slides.narration:
With this, we come to the end of this tutorial.
Let us summarise.
We learned that **LLMs** understand text via **tokens**.
**Tokenization** is the process of splitting text into these sub-word units.
And **tokens** are critical for **context windows**, cost, and efficient **chunking**.

slides.title: Assignment
slides.narration:
As an assignment, please do the following.
Find an online **tokenizer** tool.
Experiment with different types of text: short words, long words, sentences, and paragraphs.
Observe how the **token** count changes.
Try to find a sentence that results in exactly 10 **tokens**.
